scripts.title: Part 107: How far below a cloud?
scripts.q2: How far *below* a cloud must you stay?
scripts.trap: Trap: 2,000 ft is the *horizontal* distance!
scripts.explain: 14 CFR 107.51(d) requires at least 500 feet below the cloud and 2,000 feet horizontally from the cloud.

scripts.title: Part 107: Which crash must you report?
scripts.q2: Report to the FAA above what cost?
scripts.trap: Trap: $500, and your drone *doesn't count*!
scripts.explain: Report within 10 calendar days if property other than the drone has repair cost (or total-loss value) over $500 (14 CFR 107.9).

scripts.title: Part 107: Max altitude near a tower
scripts.q2: Within 400 ft of a 600-ft tower, how high?
scripts.trap: Trap: It's 400 ft above the *tower's top*!
scripts.explain: Within a 400-foot radius of a structure you may fly up to 400 feet above its uppermost limit (14 CFR 107.51(b)).

scripts.title: Part 107: Minimum age for a Remote Pilot Certificate
scripts.q2: What is the *minimum* age to apply?
scripts.trap: Trap: Just *16*, not 18!
scripts.explain: An applicant for a remote pilot certificate must be at least 16 years old and able to read, speak, write, and understand English (14 CFR 107.61).

scripts.title: Part 107: Is METAR wind true or magnetic?
scripts.q2: The 140 is measured from which north?
scripts.trap: Trap: METAR winds use *true* north!
scripts.explain: In a METAR the first three digits give the direction the wind blows from, in tens of degrees true; the last two are speed in knots. 14021KT = from 140 degrees true at 21 kt.

scripts.title: Part 107: Can binoculars keep you in VLOS?
scripts.q2: Which aid still counts for VLOS?
scripts.trap: Trap: Only *corrective lenses* count!
scripts.explain: VLOS must be kept with vision unaided by any device other than corrective lenses (spectacles or contact lenses). Binoculars (only momentarily, for awareness) and FPV goggles do not satisfy VLOS (14 CFR 107.31).

scripts.title: Part 107: Class E surface area at an airport
scripts.q2: What do you need before flying there?
scripts.trap: Trap: Class E *surface area* needs ATC OK!
scripts.explain: Prior ATC authorization is required in Class B, C, or D airspace and within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport (14 CFR 107.41).

scripts.title: Part 107: Load factor in a 60-degree bank
scripts.q2: Load factor at a *60-degree* bank?
scripts.trap: Trap: 3 G takes a bank over 72 degrees!
scripts.explain: Per the FAA study guide, any aircraft in a coordinated level turn at a 60-degree bank has a load factor of 2 G. Banking more than 72 degrees produces a load factor of 3.

scripts.title: Part 107: How often is recurrent training due?
scripts.q2: Recurrent training is due within?
scripts.trap: Trap: It's 24 *calendar* months, not 12!
scripts.explain: To act as remote pilot in command, you must have passed the initial knowledge test or completed recurrent training within the previous 24 calendar months (14 CFR 107.65).

scripts.title: Part 107: Flying from a moving boat
scripts.q2: When is it allowed under Part 107?
scripts.trap: Trap: OK over *sparsely populated* areas!
scripts.explain: From a moving land or water vehicle you may fly only over a sparsely populated area, and not while carrying another person's property for hire. Flying from a moving aircraft is banned (14 CFR 107.25).

scripts.title: Part 107: How long is a TAF valid?
scripts.q2: Each TAF is valid for how long?
scripts.trap: Trap: A TAF covers *24 or 30* hours!
scripts.explain: Per the FAA study guide, each TAF is valid for a 24- or 30-hour period. Inside it, FM marks a rapid, significant change and TEMPO marks temporary changes expected to last less than 1 hour.

scripts.title: Part 107: How high does Class C airspace go?
scripts.q2: Usual top, above airport elevation?
scripts.trap: Trap: 2,500 ft is Class *D*!
scripts.explain: Class C is generally from the surface to 4,000 ft above airport elevation (charted in MSL). Class D is generally up to 2,500 ft. Both require prior ATC authorization for Part 107 flights.

scripts.title: Part 107: Deadline to report a new address
scripts.q1: You moved to a new address.
scripts.q2: Notify the FAA within how many days?
scripts.trap: Trap: Notify within *30 days* to keep flying!
scripts.explain: If you change your permanent mailing address, you may not exercise remote pilot privileges after 30 days from the move unless you have notified the FAA of the new address (14 CFR 107.77).

scripts.title: Part 107: Does humid air help drone performance?
scripts.q2: What happens to density altitude?
scripts.trap: Trap: Moist air is *lighter* than dry air!
scripts.explain: Water vapor is lighter than air, so moist air is less dense than dry air. More humidity raises density altitude and lowers aircraft performance.

scripts.title: Part 107: Night anti-collision light visibility
scripts.q2: Anti-collision light must be visible for?
scripts.trap: Trap: At least *3 SM*, and never switched off!
scripts.explain: At night the drone needs lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles. You may reduce its intensity in the interest of safety but may not extinguish it (14 CFR 107.29).

scripts.title: Part 107: Find the ceiling in a METAR
scripts.q2: What is the *ceiling*?
scripts.trap: Trap: Ceiling is the lowest *BKN or OVC* layer!
scripts.explain: Cloud bases are coded in hundreds of feet AGL. A ceiling is the lowest layer reported as broken (BKN) or overcast (OVC). FEW and SCT don't count, so BKN030 gives a ceiling of 3,000 ft AGL.

scripts.title: Part 107: Alcohol rule - how many hours?
scripts.q2: Minimum wait before you can fly?
scripts.trap: Trap: *8 hours*, and still under 0.04!
scripts.explain: Part 107 applies 14 CFR 91.17: no flying within 8 hours after drinking any alcohol, while under the influence, or with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater.

scripts.title: Part 107: Where does Class G airspace end?
scripts.q2: It extends from the surface up to?
scripts.trap: Trap: 400 ft is your *drone* limit, not G's top!
scripts.explain: Class G extends from the surface to the base of the overlying Class E airspace; in most areas that base is 1,200 ft AGL. Your 400 ft altitude limit is a separate Part 107 rule.

scripts.title: Part 107: Flying over a person in a car
scripts.q2: You may fly over a person who is?
scripts.trap: Trap: The vehicle must be *stationary*!
scripts.explain: Without a Subpart D category, you may fly over a person only if they directly take part in the operation, or are under a covered structure or inside a stationary vehicle that gives reasonable protection (14 CFR 107.39).

scripts.title: Part 107: Which thunderstorm stage is mostly updrafts?
scripts.q2: Which stage is mainly *updrafts*?
scripts.trap: Trap: Cumulus = *updrafts*; rain comes later!
scripts.explain: A thunderstorm cell goes through three stages: cumulus (updrafts build the cloud), mature (downdrafts and precipitation begin), and dissipating (the storm weakens).

scripts.title: Part 107: Must you show your cert to police?
scripts.q2: Must you show your remote pilot cert?
scripts.trap: Trap: Police, FAA, NTSB, and TSA *all* can ask!
scripts.explain: You must present your remote pilot certificate on request of the FAA, an NTSB representative, any federal, state, or local law enforcement officer, or a TSA representative (14 CFR 107.7).

scripts.title: Part 107: What happens to stall speed in a turn?
scripts.q2: What happens to stall speed?
scripts.trap: Trap: More load factor = *higher* stall speed!
scripts.explain: Stall speed increases in proportion to the square root of the load factor. A turn raises load factor (2 G at a 60-degree bank), so the aircraft stalls at a higher speed than in level flight.

scripts.title: Part 107: Is a visual observer required?
scripts.q2: Must you use a visual observer?
scripts.trap: Trap: A VO is used only *if* you choose one!
scripts.explain: Part 107 refers to a visual observer 'if one is used.' Without one, the remote pilot in command and person at the controls keep the drone in VLOS. With a VO, all must communicate effectively at all times.

scripts.title: Part 107: What does M mean in a METAR temperature?
scripts.q2: What does the *letter M* mean?
scripts.trap: Trap: M means *minus*, temps below zero C!
scripts.explain: METAR temperature and dew point are always in degrees Celsius. Values below 0 C are preceded by M for minus, so M02/M05 means a temperature of -2 C and a dew point of -5 C.

scripts.title: Part 107: Failed the test - when can you retake it?
scripts.q2: When can you reapply to take it again?
scripts.trap: Trap: Wait *14 calendar days*!
scripts.explain: An applicant who fails the aeronautical knowledge test may not reapply for the test for 14 calendar days after failing (14 CFR 107.71).

scripts.title: Part 107: Does payload count toward 55 lb?
scripts.q2: Is it a *small* UA under Part 107?
scripts.trap: Trap: Weight counts *everything* on board!
scripts.explain: A small unmanned aircraft weighs less than 55 lb on takeoff, including everything on board or attached. 50 lb + 8 lb = 58 lb, so it is not a small UA under Part 107.

scripts.title: Part 107: Flying in a restricted area
scripts.q2: What do you need to fly inside it?
scripts.trap: Trap: Ask the *using or controlling* agency!
scripts.explain: No person may operate a small UA in a prohibited or restricted area unless that person has permission from the using or controlling agency, as appropriate (14 CFR 107.45).

scripts.title: Part 107: Can you drop an object from a drone?
scripts.q2: Is it allowed under Part 107?
scripts.trap: Trap: Banned only if it creates *undue hazard*!
scripts.explain: 14 CFR 107.23(b) bans allowing an object to be dropped in a manner that creates an undue hazard to persons or property. Drops without undue hazard are allowed, but hazardous materials may never be carried (107.36).

scripts.title: Part 107: Stable air - smooth or bumpy?
scripts.q2: What conditions are typical?
scripts.trap: Trap: Stable = *smooth* air but poor visibility!
scripts.explain: Stable air typically brings smooth air, stratiform clouds and fog, and fair to poor visibility in haze and smoke. Unstable air brings turbulence, cumuliform clouds, and good visibility.

scripts.title: Part 107: Which rule can a waiver cover?
scripts.q2: Which rule can a waiver cover?
scripts.trap: Trap: Alcohol and hazmat rules *can't* be waived!
scripts.explain: Waivers cover only the rules listed in 14 CFR 107.205, such as 107.39 (over people), 107.31 (VLOS), 107.29(a)(2) and (b) (anti-collision lights), and 107.51 limits. 107.27 (alcohol, drugs) and 107.36 (hazmat) are not listed.

scripts.title: Part 107: Drone vs. hot air balloon - who yields?
scripts.q2: Who must give way?
scripts.trap: Trap: Drones yield to *all* aircraft!
scripts.explain: A small UA must yield the right of way to all aircraft, airborne vehicles, and launch and reentry vehicles, and may not pass over, under, or ahead of them unless well clear (14 CFR 107.37(a)).

scripts.title: Part 107: CG ahead of center of pressure
scripts.q2: What tendency does the aircraft have?
scripts.trap: Trap: CG ahead of CP tips the *nose down*!
scripts.explain: Per the FAA study guide, when the center of gravity (CG) is forward of the center of pressure (CP), the aircraft tends to pitch nose down. Operating with the CG outside approved limits causes control difficulty.
scripts.basis: FAA-G-8082-22, Ch. 4 (Small Unmanned Aircraft Loading), p. 29

scripts.title: Part 107: Can a friend without a cert fly your drone?
scripts.q2: Can they use the controls on your flight?
scripts.trap: Trap: OK if you can *take control* at once!
scripts.explain: A person without a remote pilot certificate may manipulate the controls only under the direct supervision of a remote pilot in command who can immediately take direct control of the flight (14 CFR 107.12(a)).

scripts.title: Part 107: New medicine - how long before flying?
scripts.q1: You took a new OTC medicine.
scripts.q2: Per FAA guidance, wait how long to fly?
scripts.trap: Trap: 8 hours is the *alcohol* rule!
scripts.explain: The FAA study guide advises waiting at least 48 hours after the first dose of any new medication, OTC or prescribed, before flying. 8 hours is the alcohol rule. Never fly with a condition that affects safety (107.17).

scripts.title: Part 107: Minimum visibility - measured from where?
scripts.q2: 3 SM, observed from *where*?
scripts.trap: Trap: Not the airport METAR; it's *your* station!
scripts.explain: Flight visibility must be at least 3 SM as observed from the control station (14 CFR 107.51(c)): the average slant distance from it at which prominent unlighted (day) or lighted (night) objects can be seen and identified.

scripts.title: Part 107: Military training route with 4 digits
scripts.q2: Any segment above 1,500 ft AGL?
scripts.trap: Trap: 4 digits = *none* above 1,500 ft AGL!
scripts.explain: Military training routes with no segment above 1,500 ft AGL are identified by four numbers (e.g., IR1206, VR1207). Routes with one or more segments above 1,500 ft AGL use three numbers.

scripts.title: Part 107: Max groundspeed - 87 kt or 100 kt?
scripts.q2: Max *groundspeed* in knots?
scripts.trap: Trap: 100 is *mph*; in knots it's 87!
scripts.explain: The groundspeed of a small UA may not exceed 87 knots (100 mph) under 14 CFR 107.51(a). This limit is one a waiver can cover (107.205).

scripts.title: Part 107: Emergency deviation - when to report it?
scripts.q2: When must you send a written report?
scripts.trap: Trap: Only on the FAA's *request*!
scripts.explain: In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the remote pilot in command may deviate from Part 107 as needed, and sends a written report of the deviation only upon the FAA's request (14 CFR 107.21).

scripts.title: Part 107: Category 1 weight limit over people
scripts.q2: Max takeoff weight, all included?
scripts.trap: Trap: 0.55 lb *including* everything attached!
scripts.explain: Category 1 requires a takeoff weight of 0.55 lb or less, including everything on board or attached, and no exposed rotating parts that would lacerate human skin (14 CFR 107.110).

scripts.title: Part 107: How high does Class B airspace go?
scripts.q2: It generally extends from the surface to?
scripts.trap: Trap: 18,000 ft MSL is where Class *A* starts!
scripts.explain: Class B is generally from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL, often shaped like an upside-down wedding cake. Class E typically ends just below 18,000 ft MSL, the base of Class A. Part 107 needs ATC authorization in Class B.

scripts.title: Part 107: Where must the registration number go?
scripts.q2: Where must the identifier be displayed?
scripts.trap: Trap: Must be on an *external* surface!
scripts.explain: The unique identifier (registration number) must be legible, affixed so it stays on for each operation, and displayed on an external surface of the small UA (14 CFR 48.200(a), 48.205(c)). Inside the battery bay does not meet this.

scripts.title: Part 107: What location does a Remote ID module send?
scripts.q2: Besides the drone, which spot does it send?
scripts.trap: Trap: A module sends the *takeoff* spot!
scripts.explain: A Remote ID broadcast module sends the drone's position plus the latitude and longitude of the takeoff spot (14 CFR 89.315(e)). Standard Remote ID drones send the control station location instead (89.305(b)). Module users must keep VLOS.
